analogy.p: Imagine a single drop of ink on a white shirt. At first it is a small, identifiable mark (the single bloody act of Act 1 is honourable). Then it spreads, soaks through, and changes the colour of everything it touches: hands, clothes, sleep, even the weather. Macbeth's images work like that stain: once the first drop falls the pattern cannot be reversed. The analogy breaks down because ink does not choose to spread, whereas Macbeth chooses each further act.
analogy.t: A stain that spreads through a white shirt

bullets: An **image pattern** (or motif) is a group of related images repeated across the play, not a single metaphor. Always say where in the play your examples come from.
Each pattern starts in a morally neutral or positive sense in Act 1 and ends in a corrupted sense by Act 5. That reversal is itself an argument about the tragedy.
The patterns overlap: blood is a kind of clothing (it stains), darkness hides the blood, and sleep is lost because of the blood. Showing the links lifts a response beyond feature spotting.
Edexcel AO2 rewards the effect of the writer's choices on the audience, so always finish by saying what the image makes the audience feel or understand.

callouts.p: Descriptive language that creates pictures and sensations in the audience's mind, often through simile, metaphor, personification or symbolism.
Macbeth's crime reverses the natural order, so the imagery shows nature, appearance and rest all turning against him.

core.h: Why imagery matters in a tragedy built on language
core.p: Shakespeare's stage had no electric light, no scenery to speak of and no film score. Atmosphere, setting and moral meaning had to be created by words, so **imagery** (language that appeals to the senses and carries symbolic meaning) does the work that cinematography does today. In Macbeth four patterns recur so often that the play feels like a single poem: blood, darkness, clothing and sleep. The key to a high mark is that each image **changes meaning** as the play develops, so tracing the shift tells you how Macbeth and Lady Macbeth change.

bullets: **Act 1 Scene 2:** Duncan asks what bloody man is that, and the sergeant is honoured. Blood signals loyalty and courage.
**Act 2 Scene 1:** in the dagger vision Macbeth sees gouts of blood on the blade and handle. The blood appears before the crime, so guilt precedes the act.

**Act 2 Scene 2:** Macbeth asks whether all great Neptune's ocean could wash his hand clean. The hyperbole shows guilt too large for nature to cleanse. He then reverses the image: his hand would turn the multitudinous seas incarnadine, making the green one red.
**Act 2 Scene 2:** Lady Macbeth says a little water clears us of this deed. Her practical, domestic tone is the first half of an irony completed in Act 5.

**Act 3 Scene 4:** I am in blood stepp'd in so far. The metaphor of wading across a river means turning back is as hard as going on, so Macbeth is trapped by his own violence. Blood will have blood suggests a cosmic law of retribution.
**Act 4 Scene 3:** Macduff cries bleed, bleed, poor country. Macbeth's personal guilt has become the nation's wound (blood spreads from hands to the land).
**Act 5 Scene 1:** Lady Macbeth sees a spot that will not wash out, and the smell of the blood still remains. The little water has failed.

callouts.p: In the green one red, the adjective green is a natural, living colour and one red overwhelms it. Say that nature itself is stained, then link to the idea that regicide upsets the natural order.

core.p: Blood is the most frequent image and the clearest example of changing meaning. In Act 1 it is honourable: the wounded sergeant is a bloody man who bled for the king, and Macbeth is praised for his bloody deeds in battle. After Duncan's murder the same substance becomes guilt, and by the end it is something Lady Macbeth cannot scrub from her imagination. The word is the same; the moral colour is not. This is one reason the play is so unsettling: the line between heroic violence and murder is only a matter of whose side the blood is spilled for.

bullets: **Act 1 Scene 4:** Macbeth's aside, Stars, hide your fires, asks the heavens to hide his black and deep desires. Note the apostrophe (addressing the stars) and the contrast with Duncan's image of signs of nobleness that, like stars, shall shine on all deservers. The king is light; Macbeth wants to extinguish it.

**Act 1 Scene 5:** Lady Macbeth asks thick night to pall itself in the dunnest smoke of hell, so that heaven cannot peep through the blanket of the dark. The imperative mood shows her command over her own conscience; heaven is imagined as a prying watcher.
**Act 2 Scene 1:** Banquo observes there's husbandry in heaven and their candles are all out. Heaven is withdrawing its lights: an omen before the murder.

**Act 2 Scene 4:** Ross says by the clock it is day yet dark night strangles the travelling lamp. Personification of night as a murderer shows nature responding to regicide; the verb strangles echoes the human crime.

**Act 3 Scene 2:** Macbeth summons seeling night to scarf up the tender eye of pitiful day. Seeling is a falconry term for sewing a hawk's eyelids shut, so Macbeth is blinding pity itself. He has moved from asking for darkness to commanding it.
**Act 5 Scene 5:** Out, out, brief candle. The candle, a small human light, suggests life is fragile and meaningless. The pattern ends in nihilism rather than in evil triumph.

callouts.p: Malcolm's return with an army in Act 5, and the sense of dawn after the long night, restore light imagery. The structure of the play moves from darkness back to light, which supports a reading that order is restored.

core.h: Darkness and light: hiding from the self
core.p: Darkness is the setting for the crime and the cover that Macbeth and Lady Macbeth ask for. They do not just want the sun to go down; they want the stars and heaven itself to stop watching. The request is spoken, in other words it is a prayer to evil, and the play answers it by making Scotland dark in daytime. The pattern is moral as well as atmospheric: light is linked with God, kingship and truth, darkness with sin, secrecy and death.

bullets: **Act 1 Scene 3:** when Ross calls him Thane of Cawdor, Macbeth asks why they dress him in borrowed robes. The thane is alive, so the title is not his yet. The image prepares the idea of usurpation.

**Act 1 Scene 3:** Banquo says new honours come like strange garments that cleave not to their mould but with the aid of use. Banquo's image is kindly but prophetic: the garment will need use to fit, and Macbeth cannot make it fit.

**Act 1 Scene 5 and 1 Scene 7:** Lady Macbeth tells him to look like the innocent flower, but be the serpent under it, and asks whether the hope he dressed himself in was drunk. Clothing becomes disguise, and then a taunt about his courage.

**Act 1 Scene 7:** Macbeth has bought golden opinions from all sorts of people which should be worn in their newest gloss. Reputation is a garment he is reluctant to cast aside, which shows his conscience.
**Act 2 Scene 3:** after the murder he proposes to put on manly readiness. Clothing is now armour for a public performance.
**Act 5 Scene 2:** Angus says his title hangs loose about him like a giant's robe upon a dwarfish thief. Size imagery shows his moral smallness, and the word thief reduces regicide to theft.

callouts.p: Pair clothing with the false face in 1.7 and with Fair is foul in 1.1. Together they make a single argument that the play distrusts surfaces.

core.h: Clothing: titles that do not fit
core.p: Clothing imagery shows the difference between appearance and reality, and between the man and the role. In Shakespeare's time clothes announced rank (sumptuary laws regulated what each class could wear), so a robe was a visible sign of social position. Macbeth's new titles are repeatedly shown as garments that do not suit him, which tells the audience that kingship obtained by murder will not sit naturally on him.

head: Act and Scene
Garment image
Function
rows: Reputation as clothing; Lady Macbeth's taunt

bullets: **Act 2 Scene 2:** innocent sleep is described as the balm of hurt minds and the chief nourisher in life's feast. Macbeth is poisoning what he praises, a classic example of tragic irony.

**Act 2 Scene 2:** the voice says Glamis hath murder'd sleep, so Cawdor shall sleep no more. Titles stack up and each is cursed. Sleep is personified as a victim, equating the destruction of rest with the murder of Duncan, who is killed in his sleep.
**Act 3 Scene 2:** Macbeth speaks of the affliction of these terrible dreams that shake us nightly. He envies Duncan, who after life's fitful fever sleeps well. The tyrant envies the dead.
**Act 3 Scene 4:** Lady Macbeth tells him he lacks the season of all natures, sleep. Rest is the seasoning (the quality that keeps life savoury) of all living things.

**Act 5 Scene 1:** Lady Macbeth sleepwalks. Sleep, which should heal, becomes the state in which her conscience speaks. The Doctor says infected minds discharge their secrets to deaf pillows, and Macbeth's earlier prediction is fulfilled for them both.

callouts.p: Insomnia is the literal reading. The grade 9 reading is that sleep is a symbol of innocence and that Duncan, a sleeping victim, is killed at his most defenceless.
callouts.t: Do not say sleep is just insomnia

core.h: Sleep: the price of an unnatural act
core.p: Sleep stands for innocence, health and the natural order, so losing it is punishment. Macbeth hears a voice cry that he has murdered sleep, which is both a supernatural warning and a psychological truth: his conscience has made rest impossible. Shakespeare gives sleep its most beautiful descriptions just before it is destroyed, so the loss feels like a fall from grace.

bullets: Murdering a king overturns the Great Chain of Being, so nature reacts with darkness, strange events and disorder. Linking Ross's dark day (2.4) to this belief is an elegant AO3 move.
Sumptuary laws and the symbolism of robes made clothing images instantly understandable to an audience used to reading rank from dress.
Sleep and conscience matter in Christian thought: an untroubled conscience sleeps; a troubled one does not.
The play flatters James by showing Banquo, whom James claimed as an ancestor, as good while Macbeth is the usurper.

callouts.p: Instead of a bolted-on sentence beginning In Jacobean times, say: the darkness in 2.4 would have signalled to a Jacobean audience that regicide had disturbed God's order.

core.p: Macbeth was written about 1606 for King James I, who had been James VI of Scotland and became King of England in 1603. The Jacobean audience believed in the divine right of kings (that a monarch was appointed by God) and in the Great Chain of Being, so regicide was both treason and sin. In 1605 the Gunpowder Plot to kill the king had shaken the country, which is why images of darkness, equivocation and hidden knives would land hard. Use context to explain why the images are shocking, not to list facts.

bullets: Blood and sleep: after the murder the sight of his hands and the cry of no more sleep come in the same scene (2.2).
Darkness and clothing: Lady Macbeth wants night to pall itself, a word for a funeral cloth, so darkness is itself clothing.
Blood and clothing: the grooms' faces are gilded in blood to wear guilt for him; the garments of the king are disguised with someone else's guilt.
Fair is foul (1.1) is the master pattern: a day can be foul and fair at once, a robe honourable and stolen, blood honourable and murderous.

callouts.p: Always state what the pattern achieves overall: it makes the audience feel the moral cost of ambition and sees the tragedy as a corruption of the natural.

core.p: The best responses show that the four patterns are connected, because Shakespeare designs them as a system. Blood is a kind of dark stain; it clings like clothing; it prevents sleep. The characters themselves link them, for example in Lady Macbeth's idea that a little water will clear the deed, which fails when she is asleep. The pattern is also gendered: the play associates manhood with violence and sleeplessness with conscience.

bullets: Embed the quotation in your sentence: Macbeth's admission that he is in blood stepp'd in so far suggests... (keep quotations short).
Use a precise verb: conveys, implies, foreshadows, juxtaposes, intensifies.
Offer an alternative: the bloody sergeant could be read as an ideal of loyalty or as a hint that violence is the currency of Scotland.
Zoom in on connotations (strangles, scarf, seeling) rather than on the device name.
Link outwards to structure: where does the image fall, and what has changed since the last time it appeared?

callouts.p: Writing that is a metaphor, which creates imagery will earn little. Name the device only when it helps explain an effect.
AO1 argument and quotations, AO2 word, device and structure, AO3 context woven in, AO4 accurate spelling and punctuation on the Shakespeare question. Check your paper for how the marks are shared.

core.h: Writing about imagery: the grade 9 method
core.p: Examiners distinguish between students who identify imagery and those who explore it. The method has four moves: locate the image, zoom into one word, widen to the pattern across the play, then link to the writer's purpose and context. Because Section A (b) relies on recalled quotations, learn a few short phrases for each pattern with their Act and Scene, and practise using them within your own sentences.

plan: Blood begins as honour in Act 1 and becomes guilt after the murder
Clothing images show the gap between title and man from 1.3 to 5.2
Link the two: blood stains the garment of kingship
Context: divine right and the Great Chain of Being
Conclusion: the tragedy lies in the corruption of the natural
essays.q: Explore how Shakespeare uses imagery of blood and clothing to present Macbeth's change in the play.
essays.text:
Shakespeare opens Macbeth with blood that is a badge of honour. Duncan's question, what bloody man is that, introduces a wounded sergeant who has bled for the king, and Macbeth is soon praised for the same violence. The adjective bloody is therefore positive, which is crucial: when the word returns it has been corrupted, and the audience is invited to see that the line between heroism and murder is thin. In a society that rewards killing for the crown, Macbeth's later act is a perversion of the very values that raised him.

By Act 2 that moral colouring has reversed. Macbeth's dagger vision shows gouts of blood before any murder has happened, suggesting that guilt precedes the deed. After it, his hyperbolic question whether great Neptune's ocean could wash his hands clean makes the guilt cosmic. Yet the image does not stop there: the multitudinous seas would turn red, making the green one red. The Latinate multitudinous collapses into three plain monosyllables, as if language itself shrinks in front of what he has done. Nature, not just a man, is stained, which a Jacobean audience, schooled in the Great Chain of Being, would read as the inevitable consequence of regicide.

Shakespeare balances the blood with clothing imagery that exposes the same moral gap. In Act 1 Scene 3 Macbeth asks why they dress him in borrowed robes, and Banquo adds that new honours are like strange garments that cleave not to their mould. Both statements are innocent at that moment, yet they establish the idea that titles are garments that can be borrowed, loaned or stolen. Lady Macbeth then reframes clothing as disguise, urging him to look like the innocent flower but be the serpent under it. Appearance is now a costume. Although it could be argued that her language shows control, the metaphor also reveals her fear that his nature will not do what her plan demands.

The two patterns merge in the later acts. In Act 3 Scene 4 Macbeth says he is in blood stepp'd in so far, acknowledging that he is trapped; and the clothing, once borrowed, begins to be worn like a stained uniform. By Act 5 Scene 2 Angus can say that his title hangs loose about him, like a giant's robe upon a dwarfish thief. The simile reverses Act 1: the robe is no longer borrowed but stolen, and the wearer shrinks while the garment grows. Because Angus is a Scottish thane voicing a collective judgement, the moment is a verdict on usurpation as much as a description.

Shakespeare therefore uses blood and clothing together to dramatise a central paradox of the tragedy: Macbeth gains the crown and loses himself. The images do not simply decorate the play; they structure it, moving from honour to stain and from borrowed to ill-fitting. For the audience the effect is pity as well as horror, because the man who once earned a robe by blood is destroyed by the blood that earned him another.
essays.thesis: Shakespeare uses blood and clothing to show that Macbeth's ambition does not transform him into a king but exposes a man who is progressively stained and shrunk by a role that never fits.
why: AO1: a conceptual thesis (exposes rather than transforms) sustained through the whole response, with short embedded quotations.
AO2: zooms into single words (bloody, multitudinous versus green one red, borrowed, dwarfish) and comments on structure (the pattern moving through acts).
AO3: context woven into interpretation (Great Chain of Being, regicide) instead of added at the end.
Offers an alternative reading (Lady Macbeth's metaphor as control or as fear) and ends by evaluating the writer's purpose.

mistakes.w: Listing that blood, darkness, clothing and sleep appear, with no development.

mistakes.r: Embed short quotations and analyse one or two words in each.
mistakes.w: Writing the quotation out in full and then retelling the plot.

mistakes.w: Saying Shakespeare uses blood to show Macbeth is evil.

mistakes.r: Weave a precise belief (divine right, Great Chain of Being) into the interpretation of a specific image.
mistakes.w: Context bolted on at the end: In those days people believed in witches.

Quote only short phrases you are sure of and give the Act and Scene accurately.

mistakes.r: Use could also suggest to give an alternative reading, for example the sergeant as ideal or as evidence of a violent society.

quotes.a: Duncan's question frames blood as a mark of loyalty: the wounded sergeant is honoured for bleeding in the king's defence. The adjective bloody is positive here, which makes its later corruption more shocking. It could also hint that Scotland's order depends on violence.
quotes.c: Blood sacrifice for the monarch was admired in a martial culture.
quotes.ref: Act 1 Sc 2, opening of the scene

quotes.a: The dagger shows Macbeth blood before the deed. Gouts suggests thick clots, a physical word for a hallucination, and the plural implies a quantity beyond one murder. The image shows that conscience, and perhaps the supernatural, is already at work in his mind.
quotes.c: Jacobean belief that evil spirits could trick the mind.

quotes.a: Macbeth's hyperbole asks whether the whole sea could clean his hand. The god Neptune raises the scale to the cosmic, so the guilt is beyond human or natural cleansing. The rhetorical question shows he already suspects the answer is no.
quotes.c: Classical allusion typical of a Renaissance audience.
quotes.q: Will all great Neptune's ocean wash this blood

quotes.a: The monosyllables punch against the Latinate multitudinous seas incarnadine. The plain phrase green one red concentrates the image: one hand changes the colour of everything. The contrast of natural green with blood red suggests nature itself is contaminated.
quotes.c: Regicide as a crime against nature.
quotes.t: antithesis, colour imagery, contrast of registers

quotes.a: Lady Macbeth's domestic tone and the minimiser little show her practical control. She treats murder as a stain that can be washed. This is dramatic irony for Act 5, where water cannot help; the line becomes a measure of how far she has fallen.
quotes.c: Contrast with Jacobean beliefs about conscience.
quotes.q: A little water clears us of this deed

quotes.a: The metaphor of wading shows Macbeth as trapped in his own violence. The word stepp'd implies deliberate movement, so each murder was a choice, while the river imagery suggests no return. The line marks his decision to go on and shows how blood has become a place.
quotes.c: Moral point of no return; echoes the idea of damnation.
quotes.q: I am in blood stepp'd in so far

quotes.a: The imperative Come summons darkness like a servant, and thick gives night a physical density, like smoke. Her prayer to be hidden from heaven reveals that she knows the act is a sin. The sound of the plosive thick is blunt, in line with her resolve.
quotes.c: Heaven as a watching God in Jacobean thought.

quotes.a: Night is personified as a murderer and the sun as a lamp being strangled. The verb strangles echoes the human violence in the play and suggests the cosmos is suffering. Day and night are out of order, which dramatises the unnatural crime.
quotes.c: Great Chain of Being; disorder in nature after regicide.
quotes.q: dark night strangles the travelling lamp
quotes.ref: Act 2 Sc 4, Ross and the Old Man

quotes.a: The phrase makes the title a loaned garment that someone else owns. It hints at usurpation before any plan exists. Borrowed implies it will have to be returned, which foreshadows the loss of the crown.
quotes.c: Clothing and rank were publicly tied in Jacobean England.

quotes.a: The contrast between giant and dwarfish shows how the role overwhelms the man, while thief downgrades kingship to petty theft. The image is the outcome of the clothing pattern started in 1.3, and it is spoken by a former ally, which shows how isolated he has become.
quotes.c: Legitimacy and divine right: a usurper cannot fill the role.
quotes.q: a giant's robe upon a dwarfish thief

quotes.a: Sleep is personified as a victim, and the use of Macbeth rather than I makes the voice an accusation. It may be supernatural or a symptom of conscience. The line turns the murder of Duncan, killed asleep, into a murder of rest itself.
quotes.c: Sleep as a symbol of innocence in Christian thought.
quotes.ref: Act 2 Sc 2, the voice Macbeth hears

quotes.a: The fever metaphor makes life a sickness and death a cure, so Macbeth envies the man he killed. The sibilance of sleeps well soothes, creating a lull before the next violence. It marks the first moment of self-pity.
quotes.c: Death as rest in Christian thought.
quotes.q: after life's fitful fever he sleeps well
quotes.ref: Act 3 Sc 2, Macbeth to his wife

summary: Macbeth is held together by four recurring image patterns: blood, darkness, clothing and sleep. Grade 9 answers track how each pattern changes meaning across the play and use that change to explain the tragedy of Macbeth and Lady Macbeth.

terms.d: Language that creates sensory pictures in the mind and carries symbolic meaning.
A recurring image, idea or object that builds a theme across a text.
Nature reflecting human emotion or moral events, such as the dark day after Duncan's murder.
Giving human qualities to non-human things, such as night strangling the lamp.
Deliberate exaggeration for effect, as in the ocean that cannot wash the hand.
Addressing someone or something absent or non-human directly, such as speaking to the stars.
Using an object or image to stand for a larger idea, for example blood for guilt.
Placing contrasting ideas or images side by side to highlight the difference.
The ideas and feelings a word suggests beyond its literal meaning.
